correctness.rationale: In the zero-sum Euclidean hyperplane the tree incidence matrix has squared column volume n by Cauchy–Binet and its unimodular row deletions. The dual normal to the facet omitting a cut of size k is the centered indicator of a cut side, of norm sqrt(k(n−k)/n). The volume-to-height identity gives area sqrt(k(n−k)) for each of the two opposite facets. For each k≥2 the qualifying cut edges form a connected core: any edge between two qualifying edges has at least k vertices toward each. A core of h≥1 edges contributes h+1 vertices, with at least k−1 further vertices beyond each of two end cuts, so h≤n−2k+1, the path count. Summation by parts weights these tail counts by strictly positive increments. The leaves determine F₂; the star and path are the only first extrema. A nonstar attaining the second-minimum bound has just one nonpendant edge of smaller size two, giving the subdivided star. A nonpath attaining the second-maximum bound has three leaves and just one size-two cut; if two arms have length at least two they produce two such cuts, so the arms are 1,1,n−3. This shape loses only the size-two tail entry relative to the path, including at n=5; both exact gaps are twice the size-one to size-two increment. For the Cayley mean, the labeled trees with a specified one-edge split are counted by the product of two Cayley counts and k(n−k) choices of bridge. Double counting oriented sides cancels the factor two for opposite facets. Uniform Stirling reduces the kth mean summand to n^(5/2)/(sqrt(2π)k(n−k)) times 1+O(1/k+1/(n−k)); summing yields precisely the stated constant and O(n^(3/2)) remainder. This proof uses the specified metric and labeled law. The inspected check_surface.py is a finite floating-point replay and was not executed.
